contenido: 1. Peace on earth, the supreme aspiration of all humanity throughout history, undoubtedly cannot be established or consolidated if the order established by God is not faithfully respected.

2. Scientific progress and technical advances clearly teach that a wonderful order prevails in living beings and in the forces of nature and that, at the same time, man possesses an intrinsic dignity, by virtue of which he can discover that order and forge the appropriate instruments to take possession of those same forces and put them at his service.

3. But the first thing scientific progress and technical advances demonstrate is the infinite greatness of God, creator of the universe and of man himself. God made the universe out of nothing, and poured into it the treasures of his

4. It is, however, surprising the contrast that the disorder that reigns among individuals and between peoples offers with this wonderful order of the universe. It seems as if the relationships that exist between them could only be governed by force.

5. However, in the most intimate part of the human being, the Creator has imprinted an order that human conscience discovers and orders to be strictly observed. Men show that the precepts of the law are written in their hearts, their conscience being a witness. On the other hand, how could it be otherwise? All of God's works are, in fact, a reflection of his infinite wisdom, and a reflection that is all the more luminous the greater the absolute degree of perfection they enjoy.

6. But a mistaken opinion frequently leads many into the error of thinking that the relations of individuals with their respective political communities can be regulated by the same laws that govern the irrational forces and elements of the universe, whereas such laws are of another kind and must be sought only where the Creator of all has engraved them, that is, in the nature of man.

7. It is, in fact, these laws that clearly teach men, first, how they should regulate their mutual relations in human coexistence; second, how the relations of citizens with the public authorities of each State should be ordered; third, how States should relate to each other; finally, how they must coordinate, on the one hand, individuals and States, and on the other, the world community of all peoples, whose constitution is an urgent requirement of the universal common good.
8. We must speak first of the order that should govern among men.

9. In every well-ordered and profitable human coexistence, the principle must be established that every man is a person, that is, nature endowed with intelligence and free will, and that, therefore, man has rights and duties for himself, which arise immediately and at the same time from his own nature. These rights and duties are, therefore, universal and inviolable and cannot be waived for any reason.

10. If, on the other hand, we consider the dignity of the human person in the light of the truths revealed by God, we must necessarily value this dignity even more, since men have been redeemed with the blood of Jesus Christ, made children and friends of God by supernatural grace and heirs of eternal glory.

11. When developing, first of all, the issue of human rights, we observe that man has a right to existence, to bodily integrity, to the means necessary for a decent standard of living, which are, mainly, food, clothing, housing, rest, medical care and, finally, the essential services that the State must provide to each person. From which it follows that man also has the right to personal security in the event of illness, disability, widowhood, old age, unemployment and, finally, any other eventuality that deprives him, through no fault of his own, of the means necessary for his support.

12. Man also demands, by natural right, due respect for his person, a good social reputation, the possibility of freely seeking the truth and, within the limits of the moral order and the common good, expressing and disseminating his opinions and exercising any profession, and, finally, having objective information on public events.

13. Access to cultural goods is also a natural right of man. Therefore, it is equally necessary that he receive a common fundamental education and technical or vocational training in accordance with the progress of culture in his own country. To this end, efforts must be made so that citizens can rise, if their intellectual capacity allows it, to the highest levels of education, so that, as far as possible, they reach positions and responsibilities in society appropriate to their talent and the experience they have acquired.

14. Among the rights of man it is also necessary to list that of being able to venerate God, according to the right norm of his conscience, and to profess religion in private and in public. Because, as Lactantius teaches well, for this we are born, to offer God, who creates us, just and due homage; to seek Him alone, to follow Him. This is the bond of piety that subjects and binds us to Him, and from which the very name of religion derives. Regarding this point, our predecessor, of immortal memory, Leo This is the freedom that the apostles constantly claimed for themselves, which the apologists confirmed with their writings, which the countless Christian martyrs consecrated with their blood.

15. Furthermore, men have the full right to choose the state of life they prefer, and, consequently, to found a family, in the creation of which the man and the woman have equal rights and duties, or to follow the vocation of the priesthood or religious life.

16. As for the family, which is based on freely contracted marriage, one and indissoluble, it is necessary to consider it as the first and natural seed of human society. From which arises the duty to attend to it with utmost diligence both in the economic and social aspect as well as in the cultural and ethical sphere; All of these measures are intended to consolidate the family and help it fulfill its mission.
17. Parents, however, have the right to maintain and educate their children before anyone else.
18. Regarding the field of economics, it is evident that man has a natural right to be facilitated with the possibility of working and to free initiative in the performance of work.

19. But with these economic rights it is certainly linked to demanding such working conditions that do not weaken the energies of the body, nor compromise moral integrity, nor harm the normal development of youth. As for women, they must be able to work in conditions appropriate to the demands and duties of a wife and mother.

20. The right to carry out economic activities also arises from the dignity of the human person, preserving the sense of responsibility. Therefore, it should not be ignored that the worker must be compensated with a salary established in accordance with the rules of justice, and that, therefore, according to the company's possibilities, allows him and his family to maintain a lifestyle appropriate to the dignity of man. On this point, our predecessor, of happy memory, Pius So deeply is the conservation of man commanded by nature.

21. The right to private ownership of goods, including those of production, also arises from human nature, a right that, as we have taught on another occasion, constitutes an efficient means to guarantee the dignity of the human person and the free exercise of one's mission in all fields of economic activity, and is, finally, an element of tranquility and consolidation for family life, with the consequent increase in peace and prosperity in the State.
22. Finally, and this is a necessary warning, the right to private property entails a social function.

23. The right of assembly and association is derived from the natural sociability of men; that of giving the associations that they create the most suitable way to obtain the proposed goals; that of acting within them freely and with own responsibility, and that of leading them to the expected results.

24. As we already warned with great insistence in the encyclical Mater et magistra, it is absolutely necessary that many associations or intermediate organizations be founded, capable of achieving the ends that individuals alone cannot achieve effectively. Such associations and organizations must be considered as extremely indispensable instruments to defend the dignity and freedom of the human person, leaving the sense of responsibility safe.

25. The right of every man to maintain or change his residence within the geographical limits of the country must also be fully respected; Furthermore, it is necessary that it be lawful for him, when just reasons warrant it, to emigrate to other countries and establish his domicile there. The fact of belonging as a citizen to a certain political community does not in any way prevent one from being a member of the human family and a citizen of society and universal coexistence, common to all men.

26. Added to what has been said, the right to take an active part in public life and contribute to the common good is consistent with the dignity of the human person. For, as our predecessor of happy memory, Pius XII, says, man as such, far from being a purely passive object and element of social life, is, on the contrary, and must be and remain its subject, foundation and end.

27. It is also up to the human person to legitimately defend his or her own rights; effective defense, equal for all and governed by the objective norms of justice, as our predecessor, of happy memory, Pius

28. The natural rights that we have recalled up to this point are united in the man who possesses them with many other duties, and both have in the natural law, which confers or imposes them, their origin, maintenance and indestructible vigor.

29. Therefore, to give an example, man's right to existence corresponds to the duty to preserve it; to the right to a decent standard of living, the duty to live with decorum; to the right to freely seek the truth, the duty to seek it every day with greater depth and breadth.

30. It is also a consequence of what has been said that, in human society, a certain natural right of each man corresponds to the duty of others to recognize and respect it. Because any fundamental right of man derives its obligatory moral force from the natural law, which confers it and imposes the correlative duty. Therefore, those who, when claiming their rights, completely forget their duties or do not give them due importance, are similar to those who tear down with one hand what they build with the other.

31. Since men are sociable by nature, they must live with each other and each one seek the good of the others. For this reason, a properly ordered human coexistence requires that rights and duties be recognized and mutually respected. From this it also follows that each person must contribute their generous collaboration to ensure civil coexistence in which rights and duties are respected with increasing diligence and effectiveness.

32. It is not enough, for example, to recognize man's right to the things necessary for life if we do not ensure, to the extent possible, that man possesses in sufficient abundance everything that concerns his sustenance.

33. Added to this is that society, in addition to having a legal order, must provide man with many benefits. Which requires that everyone recognize and mutually fulfill their rights and duties and intervene together in the multiple enterprises that current civilization allows, advises or demands.

34. The dignity of the human person also requires that man, in his activities, proceed on his own initiative and freely. Therefore, when it comes to civil coexistence, you must respect rights, fulfill obligations and collaborate with others in a multitude of works, mainly by virtue of personal determinations. In this way, each person must act based on their own decision, conviction and responsibility, and not motivated by coercion or pressure that most of the time comes from outside. Because a society that relies only on the reason of force must be described as inhuman. In it, indeed, men are deprived of their freedom, instead of feeling stimulated, on the contrary, to the progress of life and their own improvement.

35. For this reason, civil coexistence can only be judged orderly, fruitful and consistent with human dignity if it is based on truth. It is a warning from the apostle Saint Paul: Putting aside lies, let each one speak the truth with his neighbor, since we are all members of one another. This will certainly occur when each person recognizes, in due form, the rights that are his or her own and the duties that he or she has towards others. Furthermore: a human community will be as we have described it when citizens, under the guidance of justice, respect the rights of others and fulfill their own obligations; when they are moved by love in such a way that they feel the needs of their neighbors as their own and make others share in their goods, and ensure that throughout the world there is a universal exchange of the most excellent values ​​of the human spirit. Nor is this alone enough, because human society develops together with freedom, that is, with systems that adjust to the dignity of the citizen, since, being rational by nature, he is, therefore, responsible for his actions.

36. Human society, venerable brothers and dear children, must be considered, above all, as a reality of a primarily spiritual order: one that drives men, illuminated by the truth, to communicate the most diverse knowledge among themselves; to defend their rights and fulfill their duties; to desire the goods of the spirit; to enjoy in common the just pleasure of beauty in all its manifestations; to continually feel inclined to share the best of themselves with others; to eagerly assimilate, for one's own benefit, the spiritual goods of one's neighbor. All these values ​​inform and, at the same time, direct the manifestations of culture, the economy, social coexistence, progress and the political order, the legal system and, finally, all the elements that constitute the external expression of the human community in its incessant development.

37. The current order in society is all spiritual in nature. Because it is based on truth, it must be practiced according to the precepts of justice, it demands to be vivified and completed by mutual love, and, finally, fully respecting freedom, it must adjust to an equality that is increasingly more human.

38. However, this spiritual order, whose principles are universal, absolute and immutable, has its sole origin in a true, personal God who transcends human nature. God, in fact, because he is the first truth and the supreme good, is the deepest source from which a properly constituted human coexistence, beneficial and appropriate to the dignity of man, can draw its true life. This is what the passage from Saint Thomas Aquinas refers to: That human reason is the norm of the human will, by which its goodness is measured, is a derivation of the eternal law, which is identified with divine reason... It is, therefore, clear that the goodness of the human will depends much more on the eternal law than on human reason.
39. There are three characteristic notes of our time.

40. Firstly, we contemplate the progressive progress made by the working classes economically and socially. The world of work began its elevation with the vindication of its rights, mainly in the economic and social order. The workers later extended their demands to the political sphere. Finally, they were oriented towards achieving the advantages of a more refined culture. For this reason, today, workers around the world vigorously demand that they are never considered simple objects lacking reason and freedom, subject to the arbitrary use of others, but rather as men in all sectors of society; that is, in the economic and social order, in the political order and in the field of culture.

41. Secondly, the presence of women in public life is an evident fact. This phenomenon occurs more quickly in peoples who profess the Christian faith, and more slowly, but always on a large scale, in countries with different traditions and civilizations. Women have acquired an increasingly clear awareness of their own human dignity. For this reason, it does not tolerate being treated as an inanimate thing or a mere instrument; On the contrary, it demands that, both in the sphere of domestic life and in that of public life, the rights and obligations of the human person be recognized.

42. We observe, finally, that, currently, human coexistence has undergone a total transformation in the social and political spheres. All peoples, in fact, have already acquired their freedom or are about to acquire it. Therefore, in the short term there will be no dominating peoples or dominated peoples.

43. Men in all countries are either already citizens of an independent State, or are about to become one. There is no longer any national community that wants to be subject to the domination of another. Because in our time the theories, which lasted so many centuries, by virtue of which certain classes received inferior treatment, while others demanded privileged positions, due to economic and social situation, sex or political category, are anachronistic.

44. Today, on the contrary, the conviction that all men are, by natural dignity, equal to each other, has spread and consolidated everywhere. Therefore, racial discrimination no longer finds any justification, at least at the level of reason and doctrine. This is of extraordinary importance to achieve human coexistence informed by the principles we have recalled. Because when the awareness of one's own rights arises in a man, it is necessary that awareness of one's own obligations also emerge; so that he who possesses certain rights also has, as an expression of his dignity, the obligation to demand them, while others have the duty to recognize and respect them.

45. When the legal regulation of the citizen is ordered to respect rights and duties, men immediately open themselves to the world of spiritual realities, understand the essence of truth, justice, charity, and freedom, and become aware of being members of such a society. And this is not all, because, deeply moved by these same causes, they feel driven to better know the true God, who is superior to man and personal. For all of this they judge that the relationships that unite them with God are the foundation of their life, of that life that they live in the intimacy of their spirit or united in society with other men.

46. A well-ordered and fruitful society requires rulers, invested with legitimate authority, who defend institutions and devote, to a sufficient extent, their activity and efforts to the common benefit of the country. All the authority that rulers possess comes from God, as Saint Paul teaches: For there is no authority that does not come from God. Teaching of the Apostle that Saint John Chrysostom develops in these terms: What do you say? Has every ruler been established by God? I'm not saying this, he adds, I'm not talking about each of those in charge, but about the authority itself. Because the fact that authorities exist, and there are rulers and subjects, and everything happens without obeying a completely fortuitous chance, I say that it is the work of divine wisdom. Indeed, since God has created men social by nature and no society can be preserved without a supreme leader who moves each and every one with the same effective impulse, aimed at the common good,

47. Authority, however, cannot be considered exempt from submission to another superior. Furthermore, authority consists of the power to command according to right reason. Therefore, it evidently follows that its obligatory force comes from the moral order, which has God as its first beginning and last end. That is why our predecessor, of happy memory, Pius personal, our Creator, it follows that... the dignity of political authority is the dignity of its participation in the authority of God.

48. For this reason, the right to command that is based exclusively or mainly on the threat or fear of punishment or on the promise of rewards, has no effectiveness whatsoever in moving man to work for the common good, and, even if it perhaps had that effectiveness, it would not in any way conform to the dignity of man, who is a rational and free being. Authority is not, in its substantial content, a physical force; For this reason, rulers have to appeal to the conscience of the citizen, that is, to the duty that each person has to lend their prompt collaboration to the common good. But since all men are equal to each other in natural dignity, none of them, consequently, can force others to make a decision in the privacy of their conscience. This is an exclusive power of God, because he is the only one who sees and judges the most hidden secrets of the human heart.
49. Rulers, therefore, can only conscientiously bind the citizen when their authority is united to that of God and constitutes a participation in it.

50. Once this principle is established, the dignity of the citizen is saved, since his obedience to public authorities is not, in any way, submission of man to man, but, in reality, an act of worship to God, solicitous creator of everything, who has ordered that the relations of human coexistence be regulated by the order that He Himself has established; On the other hand, by paying due reverence to God, man is not humbled, but rather elevated and ennobled, since to serve God is to reign.

51. The right to command constitutes a requirement of the spiritual order and emanates from God. Therefore, if the rulers promulgate a law or dictate any provision contrary to that spiritual order and, consequently, contrary to the will of God, in such case neither the promulgated law nor the dictated provision can bind the citizen in conscience, since it is necessary to obey God before men). Furthermore, in such a situation, authority itself completely collapses and a frightful iniquity arises. This is what Saint Thomas teaches: As for the second, human law is a law only in so far as it conforms to right reason. And thus considered, it is manifest that it proceeds from the eternal law. But, as soon as it deviates from right reason, it is an unjust law, and thus it does not have the character of law, but rather of violence.

52. Now, from the fact that authority comes from God it should in no way be deduced that men do not have the right to choose the rulers of the nation, establish the form of government and determine the procedures and limits in the exercise of authority. Hence the doctrine we have just explained can be reconciled with any type of authentically democratic regime.

53. All individuals and intermediate groups have the duty to lend their personal collaboration to the common good. From which follows the fundamental conclusion that all of them must accommodate their interests to the needs of others, and that they must direct their benefits in goods or services to the end that the rulers have established, according to standards of justice and respecting the procedures and limits set for the government. The rulers, therefore, must dictate those provisions that, in addition to their formal legal perfection, are entirely ordered to the good of the community or can lead to it.

54. The reason for being of those who govern lies entirely in the common good. From which it is clearly deduced that every ruler must seek it, respecting the nature of the common good itself and at the same time adjusting its legal norms to the real situation of the circumstances.

55. Without a doubt, the characteristic properties of each nation must be considered intrinsic elements of the common good; but these properties by no means completely define the common good. The common good, in fact, is closely linked to human nature. For this reason, its total integrity cannot be maintained except in the assumption that, taking into account its intimate nature and effectiveness, the concept of the human person is always taken into account.

56. Add to this that all members of the community must participate in the common good by reason of their own nature, although to varying degrees, according to the categories, merits and conditions of each citizen. For this reason, rulers must direct their efforts so that the common good benefits everyone, without any preference for a specific person or social group, as our predecessor of immortal memory, Leo However, reasons of justice and equity may sometimes require that men in government take special care of the weakest citizens, who may find themselves in inferior conditions, to defend their own rights and ensure their legitimate interests.

57. We must warn our children here: the common good encompasses the entire man, that is, both the demands of the body and those of the spirit. From which it follows that rulers must seek said good through appropriate means and in stages, in such a way that, respecting the correct order of values, they offer the citizen material prosperity and at the same time the goods of the spirit.

58. All these principles are collected with exact precision in a passage of our encyclical Mater et magistra, where we established that the common good encompasses an entire set of social conditions that allow citizens the expeditious and full development of their own perfection.

59. Man, because he has an immortal body and soul, cannot satisfy his needs or achieve his perfect happiness in this mortal life. This is the reason why the common good must be pursued in such ways and with such means that not only do not put obstacles in the way of man's eternal salvation, but, on the contrary, help him achieve it.

60. In the current era, it is considered that the common good consists mainly of the defense of the rights and duties of the human person. Hence, the main mission of men in government must tend to two things: on the one hand, recognize, respect, harmonize, protect and promote such rights; on the other, to facilitate each citizen in the fulfillment of their respective duties. Protecting the intangible field of the rights of the human person and making it bearable for the fulfillment of their duties must be an essential duty of all public power.
61. Therefore, rulers who do not recognize the rights of man or violate them fail in their own duty and, furthermore, the provisions they dictate lack any obligation.

62. Furthermore, rulers have as their main duty to harmonize and regulate in an adequate and convenient manner the rights that bind men to each other within society, in such a way that, first of all, citizens, when seeking their rights, do not impede the exercise of the rights of others; secondly, that he who defends his own right does not make it difficult for others to practice their respective duties, and, finally, the integrity of everyone's rights must be effectively maintained and restored if it has been violated.

63. It is also the duty of those at the head of the country to work positively to create a state of affairs that allows and facilitates the citizen to defend his rights and fulfill his obligations. In fact, experience teaches that, when there is a lack of appropriate action by public powers in the economic, political or cultural spheres, a greater number of inequalities occur among citizens, especially in our time, in increasingly broader sectors, thus resulting in the rights and duties of the human person lacking any practical effectiveness.

64. It is therefore necessary that governments make every effort to ensure that economic development and social progress advance at the same time and that, as the productivity of economic systems develops, essential services also develop, such as, for example, roads, transportation, commerce, drinking water, housing, health care, means that facilitate the profession of religious faith and, finally, aid for the rest of the spirit. It is also necessary that the authorities make an effort to organize economic pension systems so that the citizen, in the event of suffering a misfortune or a greater burden of family obligations, does not lack what is necessary to lead a decent standard of living. And the authorities must put no less effort into ensuring that workers capable of work are given the opportunity to obtain employment appropriate to their strength; that each person be paid the corresponding salary according to the laws of justice and equity; that in companies workers can feel responsible for the task performed; that intermediate organizations can be easily established that make social coexistence more fruitful and agile; that, finally, everyone, through the appropriate procedures and degrees, can participate in the goods of culture.

65. However, the general good of the country also requires that the rulers, both in the task of coordinating and ensuring the rights of citizens and in the function of perfecting them, maintain a full balance to avoid, on the one hand, that the preference given to the rights of some individuals or certain groups becomes the origin of a position of privilege in the nation, and to avoid, on the other, the danger that, in defending the rights of all, they incur the absurd position of preventing the full development of the rights of each one. Always keep safe the principle that the intervention of public authorities in the economic field, no matter how extensive and profound it may be, should not only not restrict the free initiative of individuals, but, on the contrary, must guarantee the expansion of that free initiative, safeguarding, however, the essential rights of the human person intact.
66. Government initiatives of all kinds aimed at facilitating citizens both in defending their rights and in fulfilling their duties in all sectors of social life must have the same purpose.

67. Turning to another topic, no universal standard can be established on the best form of government or on the most appropriate systems for the exercise of public functions, both in the legislative sphere and in the administrative and judicial spheres.

68. In reality, to determine what the political structure of a country should be or the procedure suitable for the exercise of public functions, it is necessary to take into account the current situation and circumstances of each people; situation and circumstances that change depending on places and times. We judge, however, that an organization of coexistence composed of the three classes of magistracies that best respond to the triple main function of public authority agrees with the very nature of man; because in a political community organized in this way, the functions of each magistracy and the relationships between the citizen and the servants of public affairs are defined in legal terms. Such a political structure offers, without a doubt, an effective guarantee to the citizen both in the exercise of their rights and in the fulfillment of their duties.

69. However, for this legal and political organization of the community to yield the advantages that are its own, reality itself requires that the authorities act and resolve the difficulties that arise with appropriate procedures and means, adjusted to the specific functions within their jurisdiction and the current situation of the country. This also implies the obligation that the legislative power has, in the constant change that reality imposes, to never neglect in its actions the moral norms, the constitutional bases of the State and the demands of the common good. It demands, secondly, that the public administration resolve all cases in accordance with the law, keeping in view the current legislation and with careful critical examination of the concrete reality. Lastly, it demands that the judiciary give everyone their right with full impartiality and without being dragged by pressure from any group. It is also a requirement of reality that both citizens and intermediate groups have at their disposal the necessary legal means to defend their rights and fulfill their obligations, both in the field of mutual private relations and in their contacts with public officials.

70. There is no doubt that this legal organization of the State, which responds to the norms of morality and justice and agrees with the degree of progress of the political community, contributes greatly to the common good of the country.

71. However, in our times, social life is so varied, complex and dynamic that any legal arrangement, even one prepared with the utmost prudence and far-sighted intention, is often inadequate to meet the needs.

72. One more fact must be added: that the reciprocal relations of citizens, citizens and intermediate groups with the authorities and, finally, of the different authorities of the State among themselves, are sometimes so uncertain and dangerous that they cannot be fitted into certain legal molds. In such cases, reality demands that the rulers, in order to maintain intact the legal organization of the State in itself and in the principles that inspire it, satisfy the fundamental demands of social life, accommodate the laws and resolve new problems in accordance with the habits of modern life, have, first of all, a correct idea of the nature of their functions and the limits of their competence, and that they also possess a sense of equity, moral integrity, acuity of wit and constancy of will to a degree sufficient to discover without hesitation what needs to be done and to carry it out on time and with courage.

73. It is a certain requirement of human dignity that men can with full right dedicate themselves to public life, although they can only participate in it by adjusting to the modalities that agree with the real situation of the political community to which they belong.

74. On the other hand, new and very broad possibilities for the common good follow from this right of access to public life. Because, firstly, in the current circumstances, rulers, by contacting and dialoguing more frequently with citizens, can better understand the means that are most interesting for the common good, and, on the other hand, the periodic renewal of people in public positions not only prevents the aging of authority, but also gives it the possibility of rejuvenating itself in a certain way to undertake the progress of human society.

75. From everything explained up to this point, it is clear that, in our time, the first thing required in the legal organization of the State is to draft, with concise and clear formulas, a compendium of the fundamental rights of man and include it in the general constitution of the State.

76. Secondly, it is required that, in strictly legal terms, a public constitution be drawn up for each political community, which defines the procedures for appointing rulers, the links with which they must necessarily relate to each other, the spheres of their respective powers and, finally, the mandatory rules that must direct the exercise of their functions.

77. Finally, it is required that the rights and duties of the citizen in their relations with the authorities be specifically defined and that the recognition, respect, mutual agreement, protection and continuous development of the rights and duties of the citizen be clearly prescribed as the main mission of the authorities.

78. However, the doctrine of those who affirm that the will of each individual or of certain groups is the primary and only source from which the rights and duties of the citizen arise, the obligatory force of the political constitution comes from and, finally, the power of the rulers of the State to command is born.

79. However, these trends of which we have spoken also constitute undoubted testimony that in our time men are acquiring an increasingly keen awareness of their own dignity and feel, therefore, encouraged to intervene in public life and to demand that their personal and inviolable rights be defended in the political constitution of the country. This is not enough; Men today also demand that authorities be appointed in accordance with constitutional norms and exercise their functions within the terms established by them.

80. We are pleased to now confirm with our authority the teachings on the State that our predecessors repeatedly expounded, that is, that nations are subjects of mutual rights and duties and, consequently, their relations must be regulated by the norms of truth, justice, active solidarity and freedom. Because the same natural law that governs the relations of coexistence between citizens must also regulate the mutual relations between political communities.

81. This principle is evident to anyone who considers that rulers, when they act in the name of their community and attend to its good, cannot, in any way, abdicate their natural dignity, and, therefore, it is not licit for them in any way to dispense with the natural law, to which they are subject, since this is identified with the moral law itself.

82. It is, on the other hand, absurd to think that men, for the mere fact of governing a State, can be forced to renounce their human condition. On the contrary, they have been elevated to such an exalted position because, given their egregious personal qualities, they were considered the most outstanding members of the community.

83. Furthermore, the same moral order imposes two consequences: one, the need for a governing authority within society; another, that that authority cannot rebel against such a moral order without immediately collapsing, being deprived of its own foundation. It is a warning from God himself: Hear therefore, O kings, and understand; Learn, you who dominate the ends of the earth. Pay attention, you who rule over multitudes and you who pride yourself over the multitude of nations. For power was given to you by the Lord, and sovereignty by the Most High, who will examine your works and search your thoughts.

84. Finally, it is necessary to remember that also in the organization of international relations, authority must be exercised in a way that promotes the common good of all, since this is precisely why it has been established.

85. Among the fundamental demands of the common good we must necessarily place the principle of recognition of the moral order and the inviolability of its precepts. The new order that all peoples long for... must rise on the indestructible and immutable rock of the moral law, manifested by the Creator himself through the natural order and sculpted by Him in the hearts of men with indelible characters... Like a shining beacon, the moral law must, with the rays of its principles, direct the route of the activity of men and States, which will have to follow its warning, healthy and profitable indications, if they do not want to condemn the storm and the shipwreck all work and effort to establish a new order.

86. It must be established as a first principle that international relations must be governed by truth. Now, truth demands that in these relations all racial discrimination be avoided and that, consequently, it be recognized as a sacred and immutable principle that all political communities are equal in natural dignity. From which it follows that each of them has the right to existence, to its own development, to the means necessary for this development and to be, finally, the first person responsible for seeking and achieving all of the above; Likewise, each nation also has the right to a good reputation and to have due honors paid to it.

87. Experience teaches that there are many and very great differences between men in science, virtue, intelligence and material goods. However, this fact can never justify the intention of using one's own superiority to subjugate others in any way. Quite the opposite: this superiority implies a more serious social obligation to help others achieve, with common effort, their own perfection.

88. Similarly, it may happen that some nations surpass others in the degree of culture, civilization and economic development. But this advantage, far from being a licit cause to unjustly dominate others, is rather an obligation to provide greater help to the common progress of all peoples.

89. In reality, there can be no superiority by nature among men, since all of them stand out equally for their natural dignity. It follows from this that there are also no differences between political communities with regard to their natural dignity. Each State is like a body, whose members are human beings. On the other hand, experience teaches that people are extremely sensitive, and not without reason, in all those things that in some way concern their own dignity.

90. Finally, truth demands that in the use of the means of information that modern technology has introduced, and which serve so well to promote and extend the mutual knowledge of peoples, the norms of serene objectivity be absolutely observed. Which does not, by any means, prohibit people from highlighting the positive aspects of their lives. But information systems that, violating the precepts of truth and justice, hurt the reputation of any country, must be completely rejected.
91. Second principle: international relations must be regulated by the norms of justice, which requires two things: the recognition of mutual rights and the fulfillment of respective duties.

92. And since political communities have the right to existence, to their own development, to obtain all the means necessary for their use, to be the protagonists of this task and to defend their good reputation and the honors that are due to them, it follows that political communities equally have the duty to effectively ensure such rights and to avoid anything that could harm them. Just as in private relationships men cannot seek their own interests to the unjust harm of others, in the same way, political communities cannot, without incurring a crime, seek an increase in wealth that constitutes injury or unjust oppression of other nations. In this regard, Saint Augustine's sentence is timely: If justice is abandoned, what are kingdoms but great robberies?

93. It can happen, and in fact happens, that the advantages and benefits that nations try to obtain for themselves compete among themselves. However, any differences that arise should not be settled with weapons or by fraud or deception, but, as befits human beings, by reasonable mutual understanding, careful and objective examination of reality, and an equitable compromise of opposing opinions.

94. To this chapter of international relations belongs in a unique way the political trend that has become widespread and imposed since the 19th century, by virtue of which ethnic groups aspire to be masters of themselves and to constitute a single nation. And since this aspiration, for many reasons, cannot always be realized, the result is the frequent presence of ethnic minorities within the limits of a nation of a different race, which poses extremely serious problems.

95. In this matter, it must be clearly stated that everything done to repress the vitality and development of such ethnic minorities seriously violates the duties of justice. A violation that is even more serious if these criminal attacks are aimed at the annihilation of the race.

96. On the contrary, it responds fully to what justice demands: that rulers dedicate themselves to effectively promoting the human values ​​of said minorities, especially with regard to their language, culture, traditions, resources and economic initiatives.

97. It must be noted, however, that these ethnic minorities, either because of the situation they have to endure unwillingly, or because of the pressure of historical memories, often tend to exalt their own racial characteristics more than they should, to the point of putting them before the common values of all men, as if the good of the entire human family had to be subordinated to the good of a race. What is reasonable, however, is that such ethnic groups also recognize the advantages that their current situation offers them, since daily contact with citizens of a different culture contributes not a little to their human development, whose own values ​​they can thus gradually assimilate. This assimilation can only be achieved when minorities decide to participate amicably in the customs and traditions of the peoples that surround them; but it cannot be achieved if minorities encourage mutual friction, which causes innumerable damage and retards the civil progress of nations.

98. Since international relations must be governed by the norms of truth and justice, they must therefore be increased through active physical and spiritual solidarity. This can be achieved through multiple forms of association, as occurs in our time, not without success, in what concerns the economy, social and political life, culture, health and sports. At this point it is necessary to keep in mind that public authority, by its very nature, has not been established to forcibly confine the citizen within the geographical limits of the nation itself, but to ensure above all the common good, which certainly cannot be separated from the good of the entire human family.

99. This implies that political communities, when pursuing their own interests, not only must not harm others, but also that all of them must unite their purposes and efforts, provided that the isolated action of any of them is not enough to achieve the desired ends; In this we must make every effort to ensure that what is advantageous for certain nations does not cause more harm than good to others.

100. Finally, the universal common good requires that in each nation all kinds of exchanges between citizens and intermediate groups be encouraged. Because, with more or less different ethnic groups existing in many parts of the world, it is necessary to avoid impeding mutual communication between people who belong to one race or another; which is in open opposition to the character of our times, which has erased, or almost erased, international distances. It must not be forgotten either that men of any race possess, in addition to their own characteristics that distinguish them from others, other and very important ones that are common to all men, characters that can mutually develop and perfect themselves, especially with regard to the values ​​of the spirit. They have, therefore, the duty and the right to live with those who are socially united to them.

101. It is a well-known fact that in some regions there is an evident disproportion between the extent of arable land and the number of inhabitants; in others, between the riches of the soil and the instruments available for cultivation; Therefore, there is a need for international collaboration to ensure an easy exchange of goods, capital and people.

102. In such cases, we consider it most appropriate that, to the extent possible, capital seeks the worker, and not the other way around. Because this offers many people the possibility of improving their family situation, without being forced to emigrate painfully to other countries, abandoning their homeland, and starting a new life, adapting to the customs of a different environment.

103. The paternal love with which God moves us to love all men makes us feel deep affliction at the misfortune of those who are expelled from their homeland for political reasons. The multitude of these exiles, undoubtedly innumerable in our time, is constantly accompanied by many incredible pains.

104. Such a sad situation shows that the rulers of certain nations excessively restrict the limits of just freedom, within which it is lawful for the citizen to live a human life with decorum. Furthermore, in such nations, sometimes even the right to freedom itself is subject to discussion or even completely suppressed. When this happens, the entire right order of civil society is subverted; because public authority is destined, by its very nature, to ensure the good of the community, whose main duty is to recognize the just scope of freedom and holy safeguard its rights.

105. For this reason, it is worth reminding everyone here that political exiles possess the dignity of the person and must be recognized with the consequent rights, which they have not been able to lose due to having been deprived of citizenship in their respective nation.

106. Now, among the rights of the human person must also be counted that anyone can lawfully emigrate to the nation where they hope they will be able to better care for themselves and their family. Therefore, it is a duty of the public authorities to admit foreigners who arrive and, as far as the true good of their community allows, to favor the purposes of those who intend to join it as new members.

107. For these reasons, we take this opportunity to publicly praise all initiatives promoted by human solidarity or Christian charity and aimed at alleviating the sufferings of those forced to leave their countries.
108. And we cannot fail to invite all men of good sense to praise the international institutions that are entirely devoted to such a transcendental problem.

109. In the opposite sense, we see, with great pain, how in the most economically developed nations enormous weapons have been and are still being manufactured, dedicating an immense sum of spiritual and material energies to their construction. With this policy it results that, while the citizens of such nations are forced to endure very serious sacrifices, other peoples, on the other hand, are left without the necessary aid for their economic and social progress.

110. The reason usually given to justify such military preparations is that today peace, so they say, cannot be guaranteed if it is not supported by parity of arms. Therefore, as soon as there is an increase in military power in some part, unbridled competition is provoked in others to also increase the armed forces. And if one nation has atomic weapons, the others try to equip themselves with the same weapons, with the same destructive power.

111. The consequence is clear: the people live in perpetual fear, as if they were threatened by a storm that could break loose at any moment with horrible force. They are right, because weapons are a fact. And although it seems hardly credible that there are men bold enough to take responsibility for the deaths and devastating destruction that a war would bring, it is undeniable, on the other hand, that any unforeseeable event can suddenly and unexpectedly cause the fire of war. And, furthermore, although the monstrous power of current military means today dissuades men from starting a war, it can always be feared that atomic experiments carried out for war purposes, if they do not cease, will seriously endanger all kinds of life on our planet.

112. Therefore, justice, right reason and the sense of human dignity urgently demand that the arms race cease now; that, on one side and the other, the nations that possess them reduce them simultaneously; that atomic weapons be prohibited; that, finally, all peoples, by virtue of an agreement, reach simultaneous disarmament, controlled by mutual and effective guarantees. Our predecessor of happy memory, Pius

113. Everyone must, however, be convinced that neither the cessation of the arms race, nor the reduction of arms, nor, what is fundamental, general disarmament are possible if this disarmament is not absolutely complete and reaches the very consciences; that is, if everyone does not make an effort to collaborate cordially and sincerely in eliminating fear and the distressing prospect of war from our hearts. This, in turn, requires that the supreme norm that is followed today to maintain peace be replaced by a completely different one, by virtue of which it is recognized that a true and constant international peace cannot be based on the balance of military forces, but only on mutual trust. We are confident that this is an attainable goal. It is, in effect, a requirement that is not only dictated by the norms of right reason, but is also in itself highly desirable and extraordinarily fruitful in goods.

114. It is, first of all, a requirement dictated by reason. In reality, as everyone knows, or should know, international relations, like individual relations, must be governed not by force of arms, but by the norms of right reason, that is, the norms of truth, justice and active solidarity.

115. We say, secondly, that it is a highly desirable objective. Who, in fact, does not yearn with the most ardent desires for the dangers of war to be eliminated, for peace to be preserved unscathed and to be consolidated with increasingly firmer guarantees?

116. Finally, this objective is extraordinarily fruitful in goods, because its advantages reach everyone without exception, that is, each person, homes, towns, the entire human family. As our predecessor Pius XII warned with words of warning that still resonate vibrantly in our ears: Nothing is lost with peace; everything can be lost in war.

117. For all these reasons, We, as vicar of Jesus Christ, Savior of the world and author of peace, interpreting the most ardent wishes of the entire human family and moved by a paternal love for all men, consider it our duty to beg and plead with all of humanity, and above all with rulers, not to forgive efforts or fatigue until the development of human life agrees with reason and the dignity of man.

118. That in the most far-sighted and authoritative assemblies, the way to ensure that international relations throughout the world adjust to a more humane balance, that is, a balance based on mutual trust, sincerity in pacts and compliance with agreed conditions, should be thoroughly examined. The problem should be examined in all its scope, so that a solid starting point can be achieved to initiate a series of friendly, firm and fruitful treaties.

120. Another principle must be indicated: that international relations must be ordered according to a norm of freedom. The meaning of this principle is that no nation has the right to unjustly oppress others or to improperly interfere in their affairs. On the contrary, it is essential that all provide help to others, so that the latter acquire an increasing awareness of their own duties, undertake new and useful undertakings and act as protagonists of their own development in all sectors.

121. Taking into account the community of origin, of Christian redemption and of supernatural end that mutually binds all men and calls them to constitute a single Christian family, we have exhorted in the encyclical Mater et magistra the most economically developed political communities to collaborate in multiple ways with those countries whose economic development is still underway.

122. We now recognize, with great consolation, that such invitations have been widely received, and we trust that they will continue to find even greater acceptance in the future, so that even the most needy peoples will soon achieve such economic development as will allow their citizens to lead a life more in accordance with human dignity.

123. But one caution must always be kept in mind: that this help to other nations must be provided in such a way that their freedom remains intact and they can necessarily be the decisive protagonists and those primarily responsible for the work of their own economic and social development.

124. On this point, our predecessor, of happy memory, Pius If it is inevitable that large States, due to their greater possibilities and power, chart the path for the constitution of economic groups between themselves and smaller and weaker nations, it is, however, indisputable - as for everyone within the framework of the general interest - the right of these to respect for their freedom in the political field, to the effective preservation of that neutrality in conflicts between States that corresponds to them according to the law of nature and nations, to the protection of their own economic development, since only in this way will they be able to properly achieve the common good, the material and spiritual well-being of the people themselves.

125. Therefore, it is necessary that the richest nations, when helping those most in need in multiple ways, carefully respect the characteristics of each people and its traditional institutions, and also refrain from any attempt at political domination. Doing so will contribute not a little to forming a kind of community of all peoples, within which each State, conscious of its duties and rights, will collaborate, on an equal basis, for the prosperity of all other countries.

126. In our times, the deep conviction has become increasingly widespread that the differences that eventually arise between peoples must be resolved not with weapons, but through negotiations and agreements.

127. This conviction, it must be confessed, arises, in most cases, from the terrible destructive power that current weapons possess and from the fear of the horrible calamities and ruins that such weapons would bring. For this reason, in our era, which boasts of possessing atomic energy, it is absurd to maintain that war is a suitable means to compensate for violated rights.

128. However, we see, unfortunately, many times how people are subjected to fear as a supreme law, and therefore invest large budgets in military expenses. They justify this procedure - and there is no reason to doubt it - by saying that it is not the purpose of attacking that drives them, but rather the purpose of dissuading others from any attack.

129. However, it is to be hoped that people, through institutionalized relationships and contacts, will come to know better the social ties with which human nature unites them and understand with increasing clarity that among the main duties of common human nature must be placed that individual and international relations obey love and not fear, because above all it is characteristic of love to lead men to a sincere and multiple material and spiritual collaboration, from which so many goods can be derived for them.

130. The recent advances in science and technology, which have had such a profound impact on human life, stimulate men throughout the world to increasingly unite their activities and associate with each other. Today the exchange of products, ideas and populations has experienced an extraordinary increase. For this reason, relationships between individuals, families and intermediate associations of different nations have multiplied greatly, and contacts between the rulers of different countries have also increased. At the same time, the interdependence between the multiple national economies has been accentuated; The economic systems of the peoples gradually become cohesive with each other, to the point that all of them result in a kind of universal economy; In short, the social progress, order, security and tranquility of any State are necessarily closely related to those of the others.

132. No era can erase the social unity of men, since it consists of individuals who possess the same natural dignity with equal rights. For this reason, it will always be necessary, due to imperatives of the same nature, to duly attend to the universal good, that is, that which affects the entire human family.

133. In the past, the heads of States were apparently able to sufficiently ensure the universal common good; To do this, they used the embassy system, the meetings and conversations of their most eminent politicians, and international pacts and agreements. In a word, they used the methods and procedures indicated by natural law, the law of nations or common international law.

134. Nowadays, international relations have undergone great changes. Because, on the one hand, the common good of all peoples poses extremely serious, difficult problems that require immediate solutions, especially with regard to the security and peace of the entire world; On the other hand, the rulers of the different States, as they enjoy equal rights, no matter how much they multiply meetings and efforts to find more suitable legal means, they do not achieve it to a sufficient degree, not because they lack will and enthusiasm, but because their authority lacks the necessary power.

135. Consequently, in the current circumstances of society, both the constitution and form of the States and the power that public authority has in all nations of the world must be considered insufficient to promote the common good of the people.

136. Now, if we carefully examine, on the one hand, the intrinsic content of the common good, and, on the other, the nature and exercise of public authority, everyone will have to recognize that there is an essential connection between the two. Because the moral order, in the same way that it requires a public authority to promote the common good in civil society, so it also requires that said authority be able to achieve it effectively. From this arises that civil institutions - in the midst of which the public authority develops, acts and achieves its goal - must have a form and effectiveness such that they can achieve the common good through the means and procedures most appropriate to the different situations of reality.

138. This general authority, whose power must be valid throughout the entire world and possess suitable means to lead to the universal common good, must be established with the consent of all nations and not imposed by force. The reason for this necessity lies in the fact that, since such an authority must effectively carry out its function, it must be impartial to all, completely separate from partisanship and directed to the common good of all peoples. Because if the great powers imposed this world authority by force, it would be right to fear that it would serve the benefit of a few or be on the side of a specific nation, and therefore the value and effectiveness of its activity would be compromised. Although nations present great differences among themselves in their degree of economic development or in their military power, they nevertheless defend, with singular energy, legal equality and the dignity of their own way of life. For this reason, with good reason, States do not resign themselves to obeying powers that are imposed on them by force, or to whose constitution they have not contributed, or to which they have not freely acceded.

139. Just as the common good of a nation cannot be judged without taking into account the human person, the same must be said of the general common good; Therefore, the world public authority must tend primarily to ensure that the rights of the human person are recognized, held in due honor, preserved intact, and actually increased. This protection of human rights can be carried out either by the world authority itself, if reality allows, or by creating an environment throughout the world within which the rulers of the different countries can fulfill their functions more easily.

140. Furthermore, just as in each State it is necessary that the relations between the public authority and the citizens, families and intermediate groups be regulated and governed by the principle of subsidiary action, it is right that the relations between the global public authority and the public authorities of each nation be regulated and governed by the same principle. This means that the mission of this world authority is to examine and resolve problems related to the universal common good in the economic, social, political or cultural order, since these problems, due to their extreme gravity, extraordinary breadth and immediate urgency, present difficulties greater than those that the rulers of each nation can satisfactorily resolve.

141. That is, it is not up to this world authority to limit the sphere of action or invade the competence of the public authority of each State. On the contrary, the world authority must ensure that an environment is created throughout the world within which not only the public powers of each nation, but also individuals and intermediate groups, can more safely carry out their functions, fulfill their duties and defend their rights.

142. As is known, on June 26, 1945, the United Nations Organization, known by the acronym UN, was created, to which other lower organizations were later added, composed of members appointed by the public authority of the various nations; They have been entrusted with missions of great importance and global reach in relation to economic and social, cultural, educational and health life. However, the fundamental objective entrusted to the United Nations Organization is to ensure and consolidate international peace, promote and develop friendly relations between peoples, based on the principles of equality, mutual respect and multiple collaboration in all sectors of human activity.

143. The decisive argument of the UN mission is the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, which the General Assembly ratified on December 10, 1948. The preamble of this Declaration proclaims as a basic objective, which all peoples and nations must pursue, the recognition and effective respect for all the rights and all forms of freedom included in said Declaration.

144. We are aware that certain chapters of this Declaration have given rise to some well-founded objections. We judge, however, that this Declaration should be considered a first introductory step towards the establishment of a legal and political constitution of all the peoples of the world. In this Declaration, the dignity of the human person is solemnly recognized for all men without exception and all the rights that every man has to freely seek the truth, respect moral norms, fulfill the duties of justice, observe a decent life and other rights closely linked to these are affirmed.

145. We strongly hope, therefore, that the United Nations Organization can increasingly adapt its structures and means to the breadth and nobility of its objectives. May the time come soon when this Organization can effectively guarantee the rights of man! Rights that, because they spring immediately from the dignity of the human person, are universal, inviolable and immutable. All the more so since today men, by participating more and more actively in the public affairs of their respective nations, follow with growing interest the life of other peoples and have an increasingly deeper awareness of belonging as living members of the great world community.

146. Upon arriving here we once again exhort our children to actively participate in public life and collaborate in the progress of the common good of the entire human race and their own nation. Illuminated by the light of the Christian faith and guided by charity, they must ensure with no less effort that institutions of an economic, social, cultural or political nature, far from creating obstacles for men, provide them with positive help for their personal improvement, both in the natural order and in the supernatural.

147. However, to imbue the public life of a country with right Christian norms and principles, it is not enough for our children to enjoy the supernatural light of faith and be moved by the desire to promote good; It is also required that they penetrate the institutions of public life itself and act effectively from within them.

148. But since contemporary civilization is characterized above all by a high scientific and technical index, no one can penetrate public institutions if they do not possess scientific culture, technical aptitude and professional experience.

149. All these qualities must be considered completely insufficient to give the relationships of daily life a more human meaning, since this meaning necessarily requires truth as a foundation; as a measure, justice; as a driving force, charity, and as a normal habit, freedom.

150. In order for men to really practice these principles, they must strive, first, to observe, in the performance of their temporal activities, the laws specific to each one and the methods that respond to their specific nature; Secondly, they must adjust their personal activities to the moral order and, consequently, they must proceed as one who exercises a right or fulfills an obligation. Furthermore: reason demands that men, obeying the providential designs of God relative to our salvation and taking into account the dictates of their own conscience, dedicate themselves to temporal action, fully combining scientific, technical and professional realities with the superior goods of the spirit.

151. It is also an evident fact that, in nations with an ancient Christian tradition, civil institutions flourish today with undoubted scientific progress and possess in abundance the necessary instruments to carry out any enterprise; but a weakening of Christian stimulus and inspiration is frequently observed in them.

152. There are those who rightly ask how this event could have occurred. Because people who profess the Christian faith and who, at least in part, really adjust their lives to evangelical norms, contributed not a little to the institution of these laws, and still continue to contribute. We believe the cause of this phenomenon lies in the inconsistency between their faith and their behavior. It is, therefore, necessary that the unity of thought and will be reestablished in them, in such a way that their action is animated at the same time by the light of faith and the impulse of charity.

153. The inconsistency that Christians too often offer between their faith and their conduct, we judge, also arises from their insufficient training in morality and Christian doctrine. Because it happens too frequently in many places that the faithful do not dedicate equal intensity to religious instruction and secular instruction; While in the latter they reach the higher grades, in the former they do not ordinarily go beyond the elementary grade. It is, therefore, absolutely essential that the training of youth is comprehensive, continuous and pedagogically adequate, so that religious culture and the formation of the moral sense go hand in hand with scientific knowledge and the incessant progress of technology. It is also necessary that young people be trained to properly carry out their tasks in the professional order.

154. This is, however, an opportune occasion to warn about the great difficulties involved in correctly understanding the relationships that exist between human facts and the demands of justice; that is, the exact determination of the gradual measures and the forms according to which the doctrinal principles and practical criteria must be applied to the present reality of human coexistence.

155. Accuracy in determining these gradual measures and these forms is more difficult today, because our time, in which each person must contribute to the universal common good, is a time of accelerated upheaval. For this reason, the effort to see how social realities increasingly adjust to the norms of justice is an everyday job. And, for the same reason, our children must guard against the danger of believing that they can stop and rest satisfied with the path they have traveled.

156. On the contrary, all men must think that what has been done so far is not enough for what needs demand, and, therefore, they must undertake larger and more appropriate companies every day in the following fields: production companies, union associations, professional corporations, public social security systems, cultural institutions, legal systems, political regimes, health care, sports and, finally, other similar sectors. These are all demands of our time, the age of the atom and space conquests, in which humanity has begun a new path with perspectives of almost infinite breadth.

157. The principles explained up to this point spring from the very nature of things or almost always come from the sphere of natural rights. For this reason it happens quite frequently that Catholics, in the practical application of these principles, collaborate in many ways with Christians separated from this Apostolic See or with other men who, although completely lacking the Christian faith, nevertheless obey reason and possess a correct sense of natural morality. On such occasions, Catholics should try above all to always be consistent with themselves and never accept compromises that could damage the integrity of religion or morals. They must, however, at the same time, show themselves animated by a spirit of understanding for the opinions of others, completely disinterested and willing to collaborate loyally in the realization of those works that are by nature good or at least can lead to good.

158. It is important to always distinguish between the error and the man who professes it, even if these are people who are completely unaware of the truth or only half-know it in the religious order or in the order of practical morality. Because the man who errs is not thereby stripped of his condition as a man, nor does he ever automatically lose his dignity as a person, a dignity that must always be taken into account. Furthermore, the ability to overcome error and seek the path of truth never disappears in human nature. On the other hand, man never lacks the help of divine Providence in this matter. Therefore it may well happen that whoever today lacks the light of faith or professes wrong doctrines, may tomorrow, illuminated by divine light, embrace the truth. Indeed, if Catholics, for purely external reasons, establish relationships with those who either do not believe in Christ or believe in Him in the wrong way, because they live in error, they can offer them an opportunity or a stimulus to reach the truth.

159. Secondly, it is also completely necessary to distinguish between false philosophical theories about the nature, origin, end of the world and of man and currents of an economic and social, cultural or political nature, even if such currents have their origin and impulse in such philosophical theories. Because a doctrine, when it has been elaborated and defined, no longer changes. On the contrary, the currents referred to, as they develop in the midst of changing conditions, are necessarily subject to continuous change. Furthermore, who can deny that, to the extent that such currents conform to the dictates of right reason and faithfully reflect the just aspirations of man, they can have morally positive elements worthy of approval?

160. For the reasons given, it may sometimes happen that certain practical contacts that until now seemed totally useless, today, on the contrary, are really useful or are expected to become so in the future. But determining whether such a moment has arrived or not, and also establishing the forms and stages with which these contacts should be made in order to achieve positive goals in the economic and social field or in the cultural or political field, are decisions that only prudence can give, a moderating virtue of all those that govern human life, both on the individual level and in the social sphere. Therefore, when it comes to Catholics, the decision in these matters corresponds mainly to those people who occupy positions of greatest influence on the political level and in the specific domain in which these questions are raised. Only one condition is imposed on them: that they respect the principles of natural law, observe the social doctrine that the Church teaches and obey the guidelines of the ecclesiastical authorities. Because no one should forget that the Church has the right and at the same time the duty to protect the principles of faith and morals, and also to interpose its authority near its own, even in the sphere of temporal order, when it is necessary to judge how said principles should be applied to specific cases.

161. In reality, there is no shortage of magnanimous men who, faced with situations that accord little or nothing with the demands of justice, feel fired by a desire for total reform and launch themselves into it with such impetus that it almost seems like a political revolution.

162. We want these men to keep in mind that the gradual growth of all things is a law imposed by nature and that, therefore, in the field of human institutions no improvement can be achieved unless it is starting step by step from within the institutions. This is precisely the warning our predecessor, of happy memory, Pius XII, left with the following words: Not in revolution, but in a concordant evolution, are salvation and justice. Violence has never done anything other than destroy, not build; inflame passions, not calm them; accumulate hatred and rubble, not make the contenders fraternize, and has precipitated men and parties to the harsh need to slowly rebuild, after painful trials, on the destruction of discord.

163. Therefore, among the most serious tasks of men of generous spirit we must include, above all, that of establishing a new system of relations in human society, under the magisterium and aegis of truth, justice, charity and freedom: first, between individuals; secondly, between citizens and their respective States; third, between States among themselves, and, finally, between individuals, families, intermediate entities and particular States, on the one hand, and, on the other, the world community. Without a doubt a glorious task, because with it true peace can be consolidated according to the order established by God.

164. Of these men, undoubtedly too few for current needs, but extraordinarily worthy of human coexistence, it is right that We publicly praise ourselves and at the same time urgently invite them to continue such a fruitful enterprise. But at the same time we hope that many other men, especially Christians, urged by a duty of conscience and charity, will join them. Because it is extremely necessary that in contemporary society all Christians without exception are like sparks of light, nurseries of love and yeast for the entire dough. An effect that will be greater the closer the union of each soul with God.

165. Because peace cannot occur in human society if it does not first occur within each man, that is, if each person does not first keep within himself the order that God has established. In this regard Saint Augustine asks:

166. The teachings that we have exposed about the problems that currently concern humanity so deeply, and that have such a close connection with the progress of society, have been dictated to us by the deep desire in which we know that all men of good will ardently participate; that is, the consolidation of peace in the world.

167. As vicar, although unworthy, of Him whom the prophetic announcement proclaimed Prince of Peace, we consider it our duty to devote all our thoughts, concerns and energies to seeking this universal common good. But peace will be an empty word until it is founded on the order whose fundamental lines, moved by a great hope, we have outlined in this our encyclical: an order based on truth, established in accordance with the norms of justice, sustained and filled by charity and, finally, carried out under the auspices of freedom.

168. It must, however, be taken into account that the greatness and sublimity of this enterprise are such that its realization cannot in any way be obtained by man's natural forces alone, even if he is moved by a good and praiseworthy will. For human society to constitute the most perfect reflection possible of the kingdom of God, supernatural help from heaven is absolutely necessary.

169. Reality itself demands, therefore, that in these holy days we turn with supplicating prayers to Him who with his painful torments and his death not only erased sins, the main source of all divisions, miseries and inequalities, but also, with the shedding of his blood, reconciled the human race with his heavenly Father, giving it the gifts of peace: For He is our Peace, who made the peoples one... And Coming, he announced peace to those far away and peace to those near.

170. In the sacred liturgy of these days the same announcement resonates: the risen Christ, appearing in the midst of his disciples, greeted them saying: «Peace be with you. Alleluia". And the disciples rejoiced seeing the Lord. Christ, then, has brought us peace, he has left us peace: Peace I leave you, my peace I give you. Not as the world gives it, I give it to you./p>

171. Let us ask, then, with instant supplications to the divine Redeemer for this peace that He Himself brought us. May He erase from men everything that could endanger this peace and turn everyone into witnesses of truth, justice and brotherly love. May He also illuminate with His light the minds of those who govern the nations, so that, at the same time that they provide them with a worthy prosperity, they assure their compatriots the most beautiful gift of peace. May, finally, Christ ignite the wills of all men to break down the barriers that divide one from another, to strengthen the bonds of mutual charity, to foster mutual understanding, to forgive, in short, all who have wronged us. In this way, under its auspices and protection, all peoples embrace each other as brothers and the long-awaited peace always flourishes and reigns among them.

172. Finally, desiring, venerable brothers, that this peace penetrates the flock that has been entrusted to you, for the benefit, above all, of the most humble, who need help and defense, to you, to the priests of both clergy, to the religious and to the virgins consecrated to God, to all the Christian faithful and nominally to those who enthusiastically support these our exhortations, we impart with all affection in the Lord the apostolic blessing. For all men of good will, to whom this our encyclical is also addressed, we implore health and prosperity from God.
